The First Amendment. Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, the First Amendment protects the fundamental freedoms of speech, religion, assembly, petition, and press from government restriction. It begins: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof, or abridging the freedom of speech or of the press, or the right of the people peaceably to assemble and to petition the government for a redress of grievances. It is the cornerstone of American civil liberties and has been litigated extensively to define the boundaries of free expression.

The First Amendment protects five distinct freedoms. Freedom of speech protects spoken and written expression, including political speech, art, and symbolic speech. Freedom of religion includes both the Establishment Clause, which forbids government establishment of religion, and the Free Exercise Clause, which protects individual religious practice. Freedom of the press protects journalists and media organizations from government censorship and prior restraint. Freedom of assembly protects the right to peaceful gathering and protest. Freedom of petition protects the right to petition the government for redress of grievances.

Landmark Supreme Court cases have shaped its interpretation. Schenck v. United States established the clear and present danger test for speech advocating unlawful action. Brandenburg v. Ohio replaced that test with the incitement test, requiring speech to be directed to imminent lawless action. New York Times Co. v. Sullivan established that public figures suing for libel must prove actual malice. Tinker v. Des Moines protected student armband protest as symbolic speech unless it caused material disruption. Engel v. Vitale struck down state-mandated school prayer.

The First Amendment applies only to government action, not private action. Some categories of speech receive no protection: obscenity, child sexual abuse material, true threats, and incitement to imminent lawless action. Prior restraint faces the highest constitutional scrutiny and is rarely justified.
